title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: The greatest improvements in the productive power of labour, and most of the skill, dexterity, and judgment with which labour is anywhere directed or applied, seem to have resulted from the division of labour. The effects of the division of labour on the general business of society are easiest to understand if we look at how it works in particular manufactures. People commonly suppose it is carried furthest in some very trivial trades—not perhaps because it really is taken further in them than in more important ones, but because, in those small trades meant to supply the minor wants of only a small number of people, the total number of workers must necessarily be small, so that those employed in every branch of the work can often be gathered into the same workshop and placed all at once before the observer's eyes.

In the great manufactures, by contrast—those meant to supply the great wants of the great mass of the people—every branch of the work employs so many workers that it is impossible to gather them all into one workshop. We can rarely see at any one time more than those employed in a single branch. So although in such manufactures the work may actually be divided into far more parts than in the more trivial trades, the division is nowhere near as obvious, and for that reason has been far less noticed.

Let me take an example, then, from a very trivial manufacture, but one in which the division of labour has very often been remarked upon: the trade of the pin-maker. A worker not trained in this business (which the division of labour has turned into a distinct trade), and unfamiliar with the machinery used in it (the invention of which the same division of labour has probably prompted), could scarcely, with his utmost effort, make one pin in a day, and certainly could not make twenty. But in the way this business is now carried on, not only is the whole task a specialized trade, but it is divided into a number of branches, most of which are likewise specialized trades. One man draws out the wire; another straightens it; a third cuts it; a fourth sharpens the point; a fifth grinds the top to receive the head; making the head requires two or three separate operations; fitting it on is its own job; whitening the pins is another; and even packing them into paper is a trade in itself. In this way the important business of making a pin is divided into about eighteen distinct operations, which in some factories are all performed by separate hands, though in others the same man will sometimes perform two or three of them. I have seen a small factory of this kind where only ten men were employed, so that some of them performed two or three distinct operations. Though they were very poor, and therefore only poorly supplied with the necessary machinery, they could, when they put in the effort, make among them about twelve pounds of pins in a day. A pound contains upwards of four thousand pins of a medium size. Those ten people, therefore, could make among them upwards of forty-eight thousand pins in a day. Each person, then, making a tenth of forty-eight thousand pins, may be regarded as making four thousand eight hundred pins a day. But if they had all worked separately and independently, with none of them trained in this particular business, they certainly could not each have made twenty pins a day—perhaps not even one; that is, certainly not the two hundred and fortieth part, and perhaps not the four thousand eight hundredth part, of what they are now able to do as a result of a proper division and combination of their various operations.

In every other art and manufacture the effects of the division of labour are similar to what they are in this very trivial one, though in many of them the labour can neither be subdivided so far nor reduced to such simple operations. The division of labour, however, as far as it can be introduced, brings about in every art a proportionate increase in the productive power of labour. The separation of different trades and occupations from one another seems to have come about because of this advantage. This separation, too, is generally carried furthest in those countries that enjoy the highest degree of industry and improvement: what is the work of one man in a primitive society is generally the work of several in an advanced one. In every advanced society the farmer is generally nothing but a farmer, and the manufacturer nothing but a manufacturer. The labour needed to produce any one finished manufacture, too, is almost always divided among a great many hands. Think how many different trades are employed in each branch of the linen and woollen manufactures, from the growers of the flax and the wool to the bleachers and smoothers of the linen, or to the dyers and dressers of the cloth! The nature of agriculture, it is true, does not allow so many subdivisions of labour, nor so complete a separation of one business from another, as manufactures do. It is impossible to separate the business of the grazier from that of the corn-farmer as completely as the trade of the carpenter is commonly separated from that of the smith. The spinner is almost always a different person from the weaver; but the ploughman, the harrower, the sower of the seed, and the reaper of the corn are often the same. Since the occasions for these different kinds of labour come round with the different seasons of the year, it is impossible for one man to be constantly employed in any one of them. This impossibility of making so complete and entire a separation of all the different branches of labour in agriculture is perhaps the reason why improvement in the productive power of labour in this art does not always keep pace with improvement in manufactures. The most prosperous nations, it is true, generally surpass all their neighbours in agriculture as well as in manufactures; but they are usually more distinguished by their superiority in the latter than in the former. Their lands are in general better cultivated, and—having more labour and expense bestowed upon them—they produce more in proportion to the extent and natural fertility of the ground. But this superiority of produce is seldom much greater than in proportion to the superiority of labour and expense. In agriculture the labour of the rich country is not always much more productive than that of the poor; or at least it is never so much more productive as it commonly is in manufactures. So the corn of the rich country, of the same quality, will not always come to market cheaper than that of the poor country. The corn of Poland, at the same quality, is as cheap as that of France, despite the greater wealth and improvement of France. The corn of France, in its corn-growing provinces, is fully as good and in most years sells at about the same price as the corn of England, even though France is perhaps inferior to England in wealth and improvement. The corn-lands of England, however, are better cultivated than those of France, and the corn-lands of France are said to be much better cultivated than those of Poland. But though the poor country, despite its inferior cultivation, can to some degree rival the rich in the cheapness and quality of its corn, it can claim no such competition in its manufactures—at least if those manufactures suit the soil, climate, and situation of the rich country. The silks of France are better and cheaper than those of England, because the silk manufacture—at least under the present high duties on the importation of raw silk—does not suit the climate of England as well as that of France. But the hardware and the coarse woollens of England are beyond all comparison superior to those of France, and much cheaper too, at the same quality. In Poland there are said to be scarcely any manufactures of any kind, apart from a few of those coarser household manufactures without which no country can well get by.

This great increase in the quantity of work that the same number of people can perform as a result of the division of labour is owing to three distinct circumstances: first, to the increase in dexterity in each particular worker; second, to the saving of the time that is commonly lost in moving from one kind of work to another; and last, to the invention of a great many machines that make labour easier and shorter, and enable one man to do the work of many.

First, the improvement in the worker's dexterity necessarily increases the quantity of work he can perform; and the division of labour, by reducing each man's business to one simple operation and making that operation the sole employment of his life, necessarily increases the worker's dexterity a great deal. A common smith, though used to handling the hammer, who has never been used to making nails, will—if on some particular occasion he is obliged to try—scarcely be able, I am assured, to make above two or three hundred nails in a day, and very bad ones at that. A smith who has been used to making nails, but whose sole or main business has not been that of a nailer, can seldom, with his utmost diligence, make more than eight hundred or a thousand nails in a day. I have seen several boys under twenty years of age who had never practised any other trade than making nails, and who, when they exerted themselves, could each make upwards of two thousand three hundred nails in a day. Yet making a nail is by no means one of the simplest operations. The same person blows the bellows, stirs or mends the fire as needed, heats the iron, and forges every part of the nail; in forging the head, too, he has to change his tools. The various operations into which making a pin or a metal button is subdivided are all of them much simpler, and the dexterity of the person whose sole life's work it has been to perform them is usually much greater. The speed with which some of the operations of those manufactures are performed exceeds what anyone who had never seen them would suppose the human hand capable of acquiring.

Second, the advantage gained by saving the time commonly lost in moving from one sort of work to another is much greater than we might at first imagine. It is impossible to pass very quickly from one kind of work to another that is carried on in a different place and with quite different tools. A country weaver who also cultivates a small farm must lose a good deal of time moving from his loom to the field and from the field back to his loom. When the two trades can be carried on in the same workshop, the loss of time is no doubt much less. Even in that case, however, it is still considerable. A man commonly dawdles a little as he turns his hand from one sort of employment to another. When he first starts the new work he is seldom very keen and energetic; his mind, as they say, is not on it, and for some time he trifles rather than applies himself to good purpose. The habit of dawdling and of slack, careless application, which is naturally—or rather necessarily—acquired by every country worker who is obliged to change his work and his tools every half hour, and to turn his hand in twenty different ways almost every day of his life, makes him almost always sluggish and lazy, and incapable of any vigorous effort even on the most pressing occasions. Quite apart from his lack of dexterity, then, this cause alone must always considerably reduce the quantity of work he is able to perform.

Third and last, everyone must realize how much labour is made easier and shorter by the use of proper machinery. There is no need to give an example. I will only point out, therefore, that the invention of all those machines by which labour is so much eased and shortened seems originally to have been owing to the division of labour. Men are far more likely to discover easier and quicker methods of achieving any object when their whole attention is directed toward that single object than when it is scattered among a great variety of things. But as a result of the division of labour, each man's whole attention naturally comes to be directed toward some one very simple object. It is therefore naturally to be expected that one or another of those employed in each particular branch of labour will soon find out easier and quicker methods of doing his own particular work, whenever the nature of the work allows such improvement. A great many of the machines used in those manufactures in which labour is most subdivided were originally the invention of ordinary workers who, being each employed in some very simple operation, naturally turned their thoughts to finding easier and quicker ways of performing it. Anyone who has often visited such manufactures must frequently have been shown very ingenious machines that were the inventions of such workers, made to ease and speed up their own particular part of the work. In the first fire engines {this was the term then used for steam engines}, a boy was constantly employed to open and shut, by turns, the passage between the boiler and the cylinder, depending on whether the piston rose or fell. One of these boys, who liked to play with his companions, noticed that by tying a string from the handle of the valve that opened this passage to another part of the machine, the valve would open and shut without his help, leaving him free to amuse himself with his playmates. One of the greatest improvements ever made to this machine since it was first invented was, in this way, the discovery of a boy who wanted to save himself some labour.

Not all the improvements in machinery, however, have been the inventions of those who had occasion to use the machines. Many improvements have been made by the ingenuity of the machine-makers, once making them became a specialized trade; and some by those called philosophers, or men of speculation, whose trade is not to do anything but to observe everything, and who on that account are often able to combine the powers of the most distant and dissimilar objects. In the progress of society, philosophy or speculation becomes, like every other employment, the chief or sole trade and occupation of a particular class of citizens. Like every other employment, too, it is subdivided into a great many different branches, each of which provides occupation for its own particular tribe or class of philosophers; and this subdivision of employment in philosophy, as in every other business, improves dexterity and saves time. Each individual becomes more expert in his own particular branch, more work is done on the whole, and the quantity of knowledge is considerably increased by it.

It is the great multiplication of the products of all the different arts, as a result of the division of labour, that brings about, in a well-governed society, that universal prosperity which reaches down to the lowest ranks of the people. Every worker has a great quantity of his own work to dispose of beyond what he himself needs; and since every other worker is in exactly the same situation, he is able to exchange a great quantity of his own goods for a great quantity—or, what comes to the same thing, for the price of a great quantity—of theirs. He supplies them abundantly with what they need, and they supply him just as amply with what he needs, and a general plenty spreads itself through all the different ranks of society.

Look at the way of life of the most ordinary craftsman or day-labourer in a civilized and thriving country, and you will see that the number of people whose industry has gone, even if only in small part, into providing him with it exceeds all reckoning. The woollen coat, for example, that covers the day-labourer, coarse and rough as it may look, is the product of the combined labour of a great many workers. The shepherd, the sorter of the wool, the wool-comber or carder, the dyer, the scribbler, the spinner, the weaver, the fuller, the dresser, with many others, must all combine their different arts to complete even this humble product. How many merchants and carriers, besides, must have been employed in transporting the materials from some of these workers to others who often live in a very distant part of the country? How much commerce and shipping in particular, how many shipbuilders, sailors, sail-makers, and rope-makers, must have been employed to bring together the various dyes used by the dyer, which often come from the remotest corners of the world? What a variety of labour, too, is needed to produce the tools of even the humblest of these workers! To say nothing of such complicated machines as the sailor's ship, the fuller's mill, or even the weaver's loom, let us consider only what a variety of labour is required to make that very simple machine, the shears with which the shepherd clips the wool. The miner, the builder of the furnace for smelting the ore, the feller of the timber, the burner of the charcoal used in the smelting-house, the brickmaker, the bricklayer, the men who tend the furnace, the millwright, the forger, the smith—all of them must combine their different arts to produce these shears. Were we to examine in the same way all the different parts of his dress and household furniture—the coarse linen shirt he wears next to his skin, the shoes that cover his feet, the bed he lies on and all the parts that make it up, the kitchen-grate at which he prepares his food, the coals he uses for that purpose, dug from the bowels of the earth and brought to him perhaps by a long sea and land journey, all the other utensils of his kitchen, all the furniture of his table, the knives and forks, the earthen or pewter plates on which he serves and divides his food, the various hands employed in preparing his bread and his beer, the glass window that lets in the heat and the light while keeping out the wind and the rain, together with all the knowledge and skill needed to make that beautiful and fortunate invention without which these northern parts of the world could scarcely afford a comfortable dwelling, along with the tools of all the different workers employed in producing these various conveniences—if we examine, I say, all these things and consider what a variety of labour goes into each of them, we shall realize that without the help and cooperation of many thousands the very humblest person in a civilized country could not be provided for, even in what we very mistakenly imagine to be the easy and simple way in which he is commonly accommodated. Compared, it is true, with the more extravagant luxury of the great, his accommodation must no doubt seem extremely plain and simple; and yet it may perhaps be true that the accommodation of a European prince does not always exceed that of an industrious and frugal peasant as much as the accommodation of that peasant exceeds that of many an African king, the absolute master of the lives and liberties of ten thousand naked savages.
